title: Repairing a sagging plasterboard ceiling
subtitle: Re-fix or replace a section of plasterboard ceiling that has pulled away from its joists, then skim and paint the repaired area
excerpt: How to repair a plasterboard ceiling section that is sagging, bowing, or has pulled away from the joists. Covers assessing whether to re-fix or replace, securing the boards, and finishing with jointing compound.
sourceNotes: Collins Complete DIY Manual (referenced, not reproduced). Reader's Digest Complete DIY Manual (referenced, not reproduced). UK trade practice for plasterboard installation and repair.

glossaryTerms.definition: A horizontal timber that spans between the wall plates at ceiling level. Plasterboard is screwed to the underside of the joists. Joists are typically spaced at 400 mm or 600 mm centres in domestic construction.

content.text: A sagging plasterboard ceiling has pulled away from the joists above: the screws or nails have failed, or the board has been wetted. The repair is to find the joists, re-fix the board securely with new screws, tape any opened joints, and skim. If the board is visibly wet, damaged, or crumbling, replace the affected section.
Find the joists and assess the board

Tap the ceiling and listen for the dull, solid sound that indicates a joist. Joists in domestic ceilings run at 400 mm or 600 mm centres. Use a stud finder or probe with a fine bradawl to confirm joist positions. Check whether the board is simply sagging or is wet and soft; press the sag gently. A firm sag can be re-fixed; a soft, crumbling board must be replaced.
Support the sagging section with a prop (a plank held up by a temporary timber prop or a hired drywall lift) while fixing. Drive 32 mm

through the board into the joist at 150 mm intervals across the full sagging section. Countersink the screw head just below the surface of the plasterboard paper but do not break through it. Fix along the full length of each joist visible in the sag zone. Remove the prop once the board is secured.

Apply self-adhesive scrim tape over any opened joints or cracks. Apply the first coat of jointing compound over the tape and over each screw head with the taping knife. Allow to dry fully (typically overnight). Apply a second, wider coat, feathering the edges well beyond the tape. Sand with the sanding pole when dry. A third thin coat (skim coat) over the whole repaired area gives the most level result before painting.

Where the board is too wet or damaged to re-fix, cut it back to the nearest joist on each side. Score the plasterboard face with a utility knife and snap cleanly. Remove the old board. Fit new 12.5 mm plasterboard to the exposed joists, screwing at 150 mm centres. Tape the new joints with scrim tape and finish with jointing compound as above.
Find and fix the cause of the leak
If the sag was caused by a water leak from the floor above, fix the source before repairing the ceiling. Patching over an active leak is wasted work.

attrs.symptom: The board sags again within a few months of re-fixing
attrs.cause: The screws were not long enough to reach into the joist, or the joist itself is damp and soft.
attrs.fix: Check the joist condition by probing with a bradawl. If the timber is solid, use longer screws (45 mm). If the joist is soft and punky, the structural timber needs assessment.

attrs.symptom: Jointing compound cracks along the tape line after drying
attrs.cause: The first coat was too thick, causing shrinkage cracking.
attrs.fix: Apply thin coats (3-4 mm maximum per pass). Allow each coat to dry fully before applying the next.

attrs.symptom: Screw heads visible through the paint after finishing
attrs.cause: The countersinking was too shallow; the screw head was not fully below the board surface.
attrs.fix: Apply a second coat of jointing compound over each screw head and sand level when dry before painting.
